chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Zayd al-Sa'igh, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I was in a town of the towns of Khurasan called Bukhara, and I saw dirhams being minted there — one third silver, one third copper, and one third lead — and they were accepted among the people there, and I used to work with them and spend them.' He said: So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem with that, provided they are accepted among them.'

I said: 'What is your view — if a lunar year passes while they are in my possession, and they contain that which makes zakat obligatory upon me, shall I pay zakat on them?' He said: 'Yes, for it is simply your wealth.'

I said: 'Then if I take them to a city where such coins are not spent, and they remain with me until a year passes over them — shall I pay zakat on them?' He said: 'If you know that they contain pure silver such that zakat is obligatory upon you regarding it, then pay zakat on whatever pure silver is yours in them, and leave aside the rest from the impurities.'

I said: 'And if I do not know what pure silver is in them, except that I know that they contain that which makes zakat obligatory?' He said: 'Then smelt them until the silver is purified and the impurities burn away, then pay zakat on whatever silver was extracted for one year.'

key_terms.الزَّكَاةُ: Zakat; the obligatory alms-tax on wealth including silver and gold
key_terms.الْحَوْلُ: The lunar year; the passage of one full year (hawl) is a prerequisite for zakat to become due on silver and gold
key_terms.الْخَبِيثُ: Literally 'the impure/vile'; used here for base metals (copper and lead) that contaminate the silver
key_terms.الْفِضَّةُ الْخَالِصَةُ: Pure silver; only pure silver is subject to zakat, not base metals mixed with it
key_terms.دِرْهَمٌ: A silver coin; the primary unit of currency in the early Islamic world
key_terms.سَبْكٌ: Smelting/casting; the process of melting down metal to separate pure silver from impurities
key_terms.نِصَابٌ: The minimum threshold of silver that triggers the zakat obligation (implied by 'that which makes zakat obligatory')

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about paying zakat on mixed-alloy dirhams containing silver, copper and lead?
ai.summary: This hadith records a practical legal inquiry by Zayd al-Sa'igh, a silversmith, to Imam al-Sadiq (AS) regarding the permissibility and zakat obligations of mixed-alloy dirhams from Bukhara, Khurasan — coins composed of equal parts silver, copper, and lead. The Imam rules that such coins may be used if locally accepted, and that zakat is due on their silver content. When the exact silver amount is unknown, the Imam instructs smelting the coins to isolate the pure silver, with zakat calculated on the refined silver for a single year — reflecting the principle that zakat applies to the zakatable commodity itself, not the mixed alloy. This narration is a significant precedent in Shia fiqh for determining zakat thresholds of impure silver coinage, illustrating the Imam's role in providing practical legal guidance to communities across the Islamic world.
